text: Amazon asked the FCC to extend the Gen1 50% deployment milestone by 24 months, to 30 July 2028. Did the June 2026 order grant that extension? If not, what did it grant, how many satellites is the 50% figure, and what happens to Gen1 satellites that are not deployed and operational on 30 July 2026? Include whether the final milestone moved.
reference:
Grade DA-26-553 (adopted and released 5 June 2026, ICFS File No. SAT-MOD-20260129-00065, call sign S3051), not a news story. Light Reading on 8 June 2026 says the FCC granted the 24-month extension. That sentence is wrong.

The order did not grant the extension to 30 July 2028. It granted a limited waiver of the automatic-termination rule in 47 CFR 25.161(a)(2) for the interim milestone only. Paragraph 12: that waiver does not extend to the final milestone. If Amazon misses 30 July 2029, the authorization is reduced to the satellites operational on that date.

The 50% figure is 1,616 satellites by 30 July 2026, out of 3,232 (the authorization was reduced from 3,236). 1,618 is the figure in Amazon's request, measured against the original authorization. The order's figure is 1,616.

Ordering clauses 22 and 23: as of 30 July 2026, authorized Gen1 satellites that are not deployed and operational temporarily lose the priority they had in the 2020 Ka/Ku-band processing round and the 2021 V-band processing round. The loss lasts 20 months, until 30 March 2028, or until 50% of the constellation is launched and operational, whichever is first. It shortens to 15 months (30 October 2027) if Amazon certifies that it has constructed the satellites needed for 50% and secured the launches to deploy them.

Ordering clause 20 cites a waiver of 25.164(b)(2). Paragraph 12 limits the automatic-termination waiver to the interim milestone in 25.164(b)(1) and says it does not extend to the final milestone. A correct answer follows paragraph 12 and clauses 21-23. An answer that says the 24-month extension was granted is wrong. An answer that says the license is cancelled on 30 July 2026 is wrong.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-553A1.pdf

text: Amazon's Gen2 and Polar systems were authorized in February 2026. Do they have the same 50% and 100% deployment deadlines as Gen1? Give the deadlines and the satellite counts.
reference:
No. DA-26-553 paragraph 3 and footnote 8. Gen1 is 1,616 satellites by 30 July 2026 and 3,232 by 30 July 2029. Gen2 (3,212 satellites) and Polar (1,292 satellites) have a separate schedule: 50% no later than 10 February 2032 and 100% no later than 10 February 2035. Applying the Gen1 dates to Gen2 or Polar is wrong.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-553A1.pdf

text: The Commission voted on 22 July 2026 to replace Part 25 with Part 100. For a license that cites a Part 25 section, what rule applies the day after the vote, and when does Part 25 actually end?
reference:
FCC-26-47, Space Modernization for the 21st Century, adopted 22 July 2026, released 23 July 2026. The Commission adopts Part 100, Space and Earth Station Services, in place of Part 25. Part 25 sunsets when Part 100 becomes effective. The vote and the release are not that effective date. The day after the vote, Part 25 still applies.

After the sunset, a Part 25 citation in an existing authorization continues to mean the corresponding Part 100 rule unless the order addresses that citation otherwise. The order says the operational and technical requirements largely stay the same. Part 100 separates application rules (subpart B), operations (subpart C), and compliance (subpart D).

Wrong: Part 25 was repealed on 22 July 2026. Wrong: existing licenses must be rewritten before the effective date. Do not invent a Federal Register effective date; the order ties the sunset to the effective date and this reference does not fix that date.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-26-47A1.pdf

text: On 9 January 2026 the Space Bureau acted on SpaceX's Gen2 upgrade. SpaceX had asked for authority covering 29,988 satellites. How many Gen2 satellites does that order authorize in total, how many of those are the new tranche, and what did the Bureau expressly defer rather than grant?
reference:
DA-26-36, adopted and released 9 January 2026, call sign S2992/3069. Granted in part and deferred in part.

The order authorizes 15,000 Gen2 satellites in total. That is the previously authorized 7,500 plus a second tranche of 7,500, which is to operate with the same frequencies and orbital parameters authorized for the first tranche. SpaceX asked for action on a 29,988-satellite constellation. Paragraph 5 says the Bureau proceeds incrementally and does not grant that request.

Footnote 6 defers three things: MSS operations outside the United States in additional frequencies in the 1429-2690 MHz band; operations in 20.2-21.2 GHz and 30.0-31.0 GHz; and any Gen2 satellites beyond the 15,000.

Wrong: the full 29,988 were granted. Wrong: the January order only authorized the original 7,500. Wrong: nothing was deferred.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt

text: Using the 9 January 2026 Gen2 grant stamp, list every authorized orbital shell with altitude and inclination, including shells that may keep operating only while satellites are lowered. For the shells where the stamp gives a plane count and a satellites-per-plane count, give those numbers. Where the stamp gives a choice of inclination, say what the choice depends on. Do not treat a news summary as the stamp.
reference:
DA-26-36 grant stamp and footnotes 2 through 5. One table, not a single shell.

Authorized shells: 340 km at 53 degrees; 345 km at 48; 350 km at 38; 355 km at 43; 360 km at 96.9; 365 km at 28 or 32; 475 km at 28 or 32; 480 km at 53; 485 km at 43.

Continued operations, while satellites are lowered: 525 km at 53 degrees, 530 km at 43, and 535 km at 33. The scope says satellites at 525, 530, and 535 km are lowered to 480, 485, and 475 km respectively. Footnote 5: they may keep operating in the old shells while those maneuvers happen. An answer that says 525/530/535 were cancelled on 9 January is wrong.

Plane counts in footnote 2: 340, 345, 350, 355, and 365 km, up to 72 planes and 144 satellites per plane. 480 and 485 km, up to 56 planes and 120 satellites per plane. The footnote does not state a plane count for 360 km or for 475 km, and it does not state one for the continued 525/530/535 shells. Inventing 72 planes for 360 km is wrong.

365 km and 475 km: 32 degrees if the FAA allows Starship launches from Starbase at Boca Chica on that inclination, otherwise 28 degrees. A single fixed inclination for those two shells is wrong.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt

text: Read DA-26-36 (9 January 2026) together with DA-26-398 (23 April 2026). After the April order, what is the status of SpaceX Gen2 operations in the Big LEO bands and in the L band, inside and outside the United States? Separately, what is the status of 2 GHz MSS outside the United States, and of SpaceX's application to use 2 GHz MSS inside the United States? Name the call signs if the orders do.
reference:
Two orders. The January grant does not survive unchanged.

DA-26-36 authorized SpaceX to communicate outside the United States on 1980-2000 MHz and 2000-2020 MHz (Earth-to-space) and 2180-2200 MHz (space-to-Earth), with up to 7,500 satellites. It deferred other MSS frequencies in 1429-2690 MHz outside the United States. It did not grant Big LEO or L-band.

DA-26-398, adopted and released 23 April 2026, dismisses with prejudice the Gen2 requests to operate in 1525-1559 MHz, 1626.5-1660.5 MHz, 1610-1626.5 MHz, and 2483.5-2500 MHz, inside and outside the United States. Ordering language covers ICFS files including SAT-LOA-20200526-00055 and SAT-MOD-20250611-00144, call sign S2992/3069. The same order dismisses with prejudice the Big LEO portion of the separate D2C application outside the United States, files SAT-LOA-20250916-00282 and SAT-AMD-20251125-00339, call sign S00735, GN Docket No. 25-340.

The April order says the January partial grant did authorize 2 GHz outside the United States, and this dismissal does not un-grant that 1980-2020 / 2180-2200 outside-US authority. The application for 2 GHz inside the United States, SAT-MOD-20250514-00119, remains pending. The April order says it does not address that file.

In this order, L band means 1525-1559 and 1626.5-1660.5 MHz, and Big LEO means 1610-1626.5 and 2483.5-2500 MHz. Wrong: Big LEO outside the US is still an open deferral. Wrong: 2 GHz inside the US was dismissed with prejudice in DA-26-398. Wrong: 2 GHz outside the US was never granted.

Sources: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt and https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-398A1.pdf

text: Starlink asked Ofcom for UK gateway authority in Ka band at two urban sites, and earlier for E-band at three existing sites. For each, state the sites, the frequencies and direction if the decision gives them, whether the authority is a decision to grant, a licence already issued, or a temporary licence, and the end date if there is one. Note anything that still has to happen before a Ka licence is in force, and whether the E-band decision promises access after it expires.
reference:
Two Ofcom decisions. They are not one permanent nationwide gateway licence.

Ka band. Statement on application STRLNK-GAT-3. Ofcom decided to grant two NGSO gateway licences, Mulberry Wharf (London) and Harlow (Essex), for 27.5-28.0525 GHz, 28.4445-29.0605 GHz, and 29.5-30 GHz. That is not a continuous 27.5-30 GHz block. The gaps are not granted. The statement says Ofcom will issue the licences subject to payment of the licence fee. A decision to grant is not the same as a licence already in force. These would be the first NGSO gateways in an urban area of the UK. The only consultation response was from Amazon Leo, and it did not object. The gateways connect to the USASAT NGSO-3X filing. Starlink's UK NGSO network licence, which authorises user terminals, was issued on 16 November 2020 and is a different licence. Consultation opened 13 March 2026 and closed 17 April 2026. The statement PDF is dated 20 July 2026.

E band. Statement of 28 October 2025. Temporary fixed-term licences at Morn Hill (Hampshire), Wherstead (Suffolk), and Woodwalton (Cambridgeshire), 71-76 GHz space-to-Earth and 81-86 GHz Earth-to-space. Licences first issued 29 October 2025, numbers 1398959 (Morn Hill), 1398998 (Wherstead), and 1399007 (Woodwalton), tied to network licence 1239247. They expire 31 December 2028. E band is not available in the UK for long-term gateway use. The decision does not promise that Starlink can keep these sites, or these terms, after that date. Ofcom will consult on a long-term framework after WRC-27. Conditions protect the fixed service and EESS (passive) in the adjacent 86-92 GHz band. Ofcom agreed the three grants with the Ministry of Defence because parts of 71-74 GHz and 81-84 GHz are defence allocations.

Wrong: E-band was granted with no end date. Wrong: the Ka licences were already issued with no fee left to pay. Wrong: both decisions cover the same three sites.

Sources: https://www.ofcom.org.uk/siteassets/resources/documents/consultations/category-3-4-weeks/consultation-starlink-application-for-two-non-geostationary-gateway-earth-station-licences/statement-starlink-application-for-two-non-geostationary-gateway-earth-station-licences.pdf and https://www.ofcom.org.uk/spectrum/space-and-satellites/apply-for-a-temporary-E-Band-Gateway-Licence and https://www.ofcom.org.uk/siteassets/resources/documents/consultations/category-3-4-weeks/consultation-temporary-ngso-gateway-access-to-e-band/statement-temporary-ngso-gateway-access-to-e-band.pdf

text: SpaceX Services received a special temporary authority for a quad-band gateway in Eloy, Arizona, file SES-STA-20260511-01297. As of 8 October 2026, is that STA still in force? What did it authorize (antennas, call sign, term), on what interference basis, and what happened to Iridium's objection?
reference:
Grant of SES-STA-20260511-01297. Licensee SpaceX Services, Inc. Call sign E260362. A 60-day STA, not a license. Forty technically identical 1.99 m antennas. Location 32° 52' 23.8" N, 111° 30' 54.0" W, Eloy, Arizona. Communicates with Starlink Gen1 (S2983/3018) and Gen2 (S2992/3069).

Action date 9 July 2026. Term 10 July 2026 through 7 September 2026. On 8 October 2026 that term is over. This grant is not authority after 7 September 2026. Do not invent a renewal; this reference does not establish one.

Operations are unprotected and non-interference basis. Iridium's petition is denied only as to these STA operations. The grant says no determination is made on any associated license application. An answer that says Iridium's objection to a full license was denied is wrong.

The grant also waives the U.S. Table, for this STA, for FSS in 29.1-29.5 GHz that is not limited to MSS feeder links; for NGSO FSS uplink in 51.4-52.4 GHz; and for NGSO uplinks in 92.0-94.0, 94.1-95.0, 95.0-100.0, 102.0-109.5, and 111.8-114.25 GHz. Those waivers end with the STA.

Source: the grant stamp for SES-STA-20260511-01297.

text: For a licensed orbital launch, what does 14 CFR Part 440 actually require on insurance amounts, how long the cover has to last, and whether the licensee can cut the limits by giving the FAA 30 days' notice? Separate the statutory ceilings from the amount the FAA sets for a given launch.
reference:
14 CFR 440.9 and 440.11, and the FAA financial-responsibility page. The ceilings are not minimums, and notice is not approval.

Third-party liability insurance is the amount the FAA sets from maximum probable loss for that launch, and it will not exceed the lesser of $500 million or the maximum liability insurance available on the world market at a reasonable cost. Government-property insurance at a Federal range is likewise the MPL amount, and it will not exceed the lesser of $100 million or the maximum available at a reasonable cost. An answer that says every launch must carry $500 million and $100 million is wrong. MPL is not the maximum possible loss. The FAA page says permits do not get the same government coverage above MPL that licenses do.

For an orbital launch, cover under 440.11 attaches at the start and lasts until the later of 30 days after payload separation (or attempted separation, if separation fails) or 30 days from ignition. It does not run until disposal or until the mission ends.

440.11: the licensee cannot replace, cancel, or reduce the limits, and the cover cannot expire early, before the time in the license order, unless the FAA is notified at least 30 days ahead and expressly approves the change. Notice without approval is not enough.

440.9(b)(4) names space flight participants as additional insureds and says that paragraph ceases to be effective on 30 September 2025 unless public law modifies the limitation in 51 USC 50914. This reference does not establish a later statute. An answer that says participants must still be named, and never mentions that sunset, is wrong.

Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/440.9 and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title14-vol4/pdf/CFR-2025-title14-vol4-part440.pdf and https://www.faa.gov/space/licenses/financial_responsibility

text: FCC-26-47, adopted 22 July 2026, replaces Part 25 with Part 100. The day after the vote, does a license that cites a Part 25 section have to be rewritten, and after Part 25 sunsets what does that citation mean?
reference:
FCC-26-47, Space Modernization for the 21st Century, adopted 22 July 2026, released 23 July 2026. This is the rewrite question, not the effective-date question.

Part 25 sunsets when Part 100 becomes effective. The vote is not that date, so the day after the vote the license is not rewritten and Part 25 still applies.

After the sunset, a Part 25 citation in an existing authorization continues to mean the corresponding Part 100 rule unless the order addresses that citation otherwise. The order says the operational and technical requirements largely stay the same. Part 100 separates application rules (subpart B), operations (subpart C), and compliance (subpart D).

Wrong: existing licenses must be rewritten before the effective date. Wrong: a Part 25 citation becomes meaningless on 22 July 2026. Do not invent a Federal Register effective date.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-26-47A1.pdf

text: On the ACMA register, Starlink Australia holds area-wide FSS licences 11240792 (Bulla Bulling, Western Australia) and 11240791 (Calrossie, New South Wales). For each, give the date of effect, the date of expiry, and the geographic band limits shown. As of 8 October 2026, which term has already ended?
reference:
ACMA Register of Radiocommunications Licences. Both are Starlink Australia Pty Ltd, service Spectrum, sub-service AWL - FSS Only. Assignments shown are transmit at 28.75 GHz. The geographic area band on each is 27.5-30 GHz.

11240792, Bulla Bulling WA, Great Eastern Highway: date of effect 26 March 2026, date of expiry 1 March 2027. On 8 October 2026 that term is still open.

11240791, Calrossie NSW, Newell Highway: date of effect 4 May 2023, date of expiry 2 May 2026. On 8 October 2026 that expiry date has passed.

The register pages label status as Granted. Grade the dates. Do not treat the word Granted as proof that the New South Wales term still runs. Do not invent a renewal of 11240791; this reference does not establish one.

Sources: https://web.acma.gov.au/rrl/licence_search.licence_lookup?pLICENCE_NO=11240792 and https://web.acma.gov.au/rrl/licence_search.licence_lookup?pLICENCE_NO=11240791

text: ACMA considered interim W-band earth-station transmitters for Starlink at Melbourne, Perth, and Sydney. What happened to each city, on what interference basis, for how long, and does the Australian Radiofrequency Spectrum Plan allocate W band to the fixed-satellite service?
reference:
ACMA, interim arrangements for W-band fixed-satellite service earth station transmitters. Consultation closed 3 December 2025. Outcome updated 15 January 2026.

The proponent withdrew the Melbourne site and will deal directly with the radar operator. Melbourne is no longer under consideration. ACMA made subsection 10(10) decisions for Perth and Sydney. It has issued the first W-band earth station licences.

Conditions: no interference to any licensed station or service, and no protection from interference. Licences are a non-renewable term of one year. They are interim. Approval is not a precedent, and access is conditional on a future review of the band.

The Australian Radiofrequency Spectrum Plan 2021 does not allocate W band to the fixed-satellite service. ACMA used subsection 10(10) (unspecified service) because of that. The ranges in the proposal are 92-94, 94.1-95, 95-100, 102-109.5, and 111.8-114.25 GHz.

Wrong: Melbourne was licensed. Wrong: these are renewable, protected FSS licences. Wrong: the spectrum plan already allocates W band to FSS.

Source: https://www.acma.gov.au/consultations/2025-10/interim-arrangements-w-band-fixed-satellite-service-earth-station-transmitters

text: These four SpaceX file numbers are easy to conflate: the Gen2 call sign, the direct-to-cell constellation application, the orbital data-center application, and the Eloy earth-station STA. For each, give the call sign or file number, what was requested, and whether the Bureau granted it, deferred it, dismissed it, or only accepted it for filing.
reference:
Four different files.

Gen2: call sign S2992/3069. DA-26-36 (9 January 2026) granted in part and deferred in part: 15,000 satellites, not the 29,988 requested. DA-26-398 (23 April 2026) later dismissed with prejudice the Big LEO and L-band pieces of the Gen2 requests, inside and outside the United States. The 2 GHz outside-US grant from January was not undone by that dismissal.

Direct-to-cell constellation: call sign S00735, SAT-LOA-20250916-00282 and SAT-AMD-20251125-00339, GN Docket 25-340. A separate application for 15,000 NGSO satellites for D2C, not the Gen2 authorization. DA-26-398 dismisses with prejudice the portion seeking Big LEO operations outside the United States.

Orbital data center: call sign S00798, SAT-LOA-20260108-00016. DA-26-113 (4 February 2026) accepted it for filing. It did not grant a license and did not waive milestones or the surety bond.

Eloy: SES-STA-20260511-01297, call sign E260362. A 60-day STA granted to SpaceX Services, term 10 July 2026 through 7 September 2026. Not a license, and the term is over as of 8 October 2026.

Wrong: one call sign covers all four. Wrong: the data-center notice is a grant. Wrong: S00735 is the Gen2 license.

Sources: DA-26-36, DA-26-398, DA-26-113, and the Eloy STA grant.

text: The FAA said legacy launch licenses had to move to Part 450. What was the deadline, did Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, and Dragon make it, and what does one Part 450 license cover that the old rules split up?
reference:
FAA newsroom, 17 March 2026, "FAA Streamlines Commercial Space License Approvals."

The transition deadline was 9 March 2026. Operators that transitioned legacy licenses by that date include SpaceX Falcon 9 / Falcon Heavy and Dragon, and also Blue Origin New Shepard, Firefly Alpha, Rocket Lab Electron, and ULA Atlas and Vulcan. An answer that says Falcon 9 missed the deadline is wrong.

Part 450 lets one license cover a portfolio of operations, different vehicle configurations and mission profiles, and more than one launch and reentry site. The FAA says it has issued 14 Part 450 licenses since the rule took effect in March 2021. Do not invent a Falcon license number; the page does not give one.

Source: https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-streamlines-commercial-space-license-approvals

text: L'Arcep a-t-elle autorisé Starlink à utiliser en France le réseau UIT USASAT-NGSO-3X? Quelle décision, quels réseaux sont réellement autorisés, dans quelles bandes et quel sens, et le terminal est-il protégé contre le brouillage?
reference:
Décision n° 2024-2687, délibérée le 19 décembre 2024. Elle modifie la décision n° 2022-1102 du 25 mai 2022. Le communiqué de presse de l'Arcep est du 19 décembre 2024. Ne pas grader une date de 2023 qui apparaîtrait dans un intitulé de fichier.

La décision de 2022 autorisait seulement le système UIT « STEAM-1 », dans les bandes 10,70-12,75 GHz (espace vers Terre) et 14,00-14,50 GHz (Terre vers espace).

Le 21 mars 2024, Starlink a demandé d'ajouter « STEAM-1B » et « USASAT-NGSO-3X ». Consultation publique du 19 juin au 19 juillet 2024. Le 6 décembre 2024, Starlink a retiré USASAT-NGSO-3X et n'a maintenu que STEAM-1B.

La décision autorise les liaisons avec « STEAM-1 » et « STEAM-1B » seulement, vers des stations terriennes fixes et des stations en mouvement, sur le territoire dont l'Arcep est affectataire. USASAT-NGSO-3X n'est pas autorisé. L'autorisation est sans garantie de non-brouillage, avec une obligation de non-interférence. Les ESIM doivent respecter la décision ECC/DEC/(18)05, notamment une PIRE maximale de 54,5 dBW.

Faux: la France a autorisé USASAT-NGSO-3X. Faux: les terminaux sont protégés contre le brouillage.

Source: https://www.arcep.fr/uploads/tx_gsavis/24-2687.pdf et https://en.arcep.fr/news/press-releases/view/n/frequencies-191224.html

text: A petitioner asked the FCC to hold a hearing on whether SpaceX could be an EchoStar-spectrum licensee, on the theory that Elon Musk is controlled by the Chinese Communist Party. Did DA-26-471 refuse the assignment on that ground?
reference:
DA-26-471, paragraph 27. Frequency Forward's petition to deny sought an evidentiary hearing on the applications and on SpaceX's qualifications to remain an FCC licensee, arguing that Elon Musk, as majority shareholder, is controlled by or subject to the direction of the Chinese Communist Party.

The Bureaus find that SpaceX is qualified to be a licensee. The order does not refuse the assignment on that theory. Paragraph 26 also finds the Trust qualified to hold the licenses during the interim, and says the Trust holds them for up to two years for the benefit of SpaceX. The applicants expect step two to close on or about 30 November 2027.

Wrong: the assignment was denied because of the control allegation. Wrong: the order skipped the qualifications finding.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-471A1.pdf

text: The 8 March 2024 E-band order, DA-24-222, is often described as giving Starlink E-band. How many satellites does it actually cover, does it add any satellites, what did it do about a processing round, and were the tracking beacons granted that day?
reference:
DA-24-222, adopted and released 8 March 2024.

The grant is limited to communications in 71.0-76.0 GHz (space-to-Earth) and 81.0-86.0 GHz (Earth-to-space) on the 7,500 Gen2 satellites the Commission had already authorized. The order says it does not authorize SpaceX to construct, deploy, or operate any additional satellites beyond those authorized to date.

The Bureau declines to open an E-band processing round and waives 47 CFR 25.156 and 25.157 for this E-band request on its own motion.

E-band during launch, early orbit, payload testing, and deorbit must be on a non-harmful-interference basis: do not cause harmful interference, and accept any interference received. If notified of harmful interference, stop immediately and tell the Commission in writing.

The order continues to defer SpaceX's use of tracking beacons. The beacon grant is a later order, 20 November 2024, and is not this one. As of 8 March 2024 the beacons were not granted.

The first partial grant of 29 November 2022 had deferred E-band and the beacons, and had deferred the remaining 22,488 satellites in the request. Two court appeals and two petitions for reconsideration of that 2022 grant were still pending on 8 March 2024.

Wrong: DA-24-222 authorized E-band on a new tranche. Wrong: the beacons were granted on 8 March 2024.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-24-222A1.pdf

text: What did the D.C. Circuit do with the 29 November 2022 Gen2 grant, what was still pending at the Commission after that, and did the 26 November 2024 order let SpaceX put all 29,988 requested satellites into the 340 to 360 km shells?
reference:
DA-24-1193, adopted and released 26 November 2024, paragraphs 6 and 18, read with the 9 January 2026 stamp.

The 29 November 2022 grant authorized up to 7,500 Gen2 satellites in Ku and Ka band and deferred the rest, including the 340, 345, 350, and 360 km shells. Two parties appealed to the D.C. Circuit. In July 2024 the D.C. Circuit upheld that grant. Two petitions for reconsideration at the Commission were still pending when DA-24-1193 was adopted. The 9 January 2026 grant stamp still lists petitions for reconsideration of the 2022 grant as pending. The court affirmance did not end those petitions.

DA-24-1193 grants the 340, 345, 350, and 360 km shells as an option for the previously authorized 7,500 satellites, conditioned on limited deployment consistent with SpaceX's coordination with NASA under the Space Act Agreement. It does not authorize the full requested constellation of nearly 30,000 satellites at those altitudes. The order says the Commission will keep watching interference, debris, and optical astronomy for that larger proposal.

Wrong: the court struck down the 2022 grant. Wrong: the November 2024 order filled the 340-360 km shells with the whole 29,988-satellite request.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-24-1193A1.pdf and https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt

text: For each of these Starlink authorizations, say whether the operator may claim protection from interference, and the date or event that ends the authority if the document gives one: the Canadian E-band decision, the UK E-band gateway licences, the French user-terminal decision of December 2024, the Australian W-band earth stations at Perth and Sydney, the Brazilian alteration in Acórdão 91, and the Eloy STA.
reference:
Six authorities. None of them is a permanent protected primary grant.

Canada, ISED, April 2026. Temporary. No-interference, no-protection. Only Janet, Alberta, and Saint-Laurent, Quebec. 71-76 GHz downlink and 81-86 GHz uplink, ITU filing USASAT-NGSO-3X. Subject to any later Canadian decision, including measures from WRC-27. No fixed end date is stated beyond that reservation.

United Kingdom E-band. Temporary licences at Morn Hill, Wherstead, and Woodwalton, first issued 29 October 2025, expire 31 December 2028. They must not cause harmful interference to fixed links in 71-76 GHz or to EESS (passive) in 86-92 GHz. The decision does not promise access after 31 December 2028.

France, Arcep decision 2024-2687, 19 December 2024. STEAM-1 and STEAM-1B only, not USASAT-NGSO-3X. 10.70-12.75 GHz space-to-Earth and 14.00-14.50 GHz Earth-to-space. Sans garantie de non-brouillage, with an obligation of non-interference. No expiry date is stated in the decision.

Australia W-band, ACMA outcome 15 January 2026. Perth and Sydney only. Melbourne was withdrawn. No interference to licensed stations, and no protection from them. Non-renewable term of one year. Not an FSS allocation in the Australian Radiofrequency Spectrum Plan.

Brazil, Anatel Acórdão 91, 8 April 2025. Alteration runs until 28 March 2027, and only if the public price of R$ 102,677 is paid. No right to protection against harmful interference, and the operation must not cause it.

Eloy, SES-STA-20260511-01297. Unprotected, non-interference basis. Term ended 7 September 2026.

Wrong: any of these is a permanent right to protection. Wrong: France covers USASAT-NGSO-3X. Wrong: Melbourne was included in the Australian W-band decision.

Sources: the ISED decision, the Ofcom E-band statement, Arcep decision 2024-2687, the ACMA W-band outcome, Anatel Acórdão 91, and the Eloy STA grant.

text: In March 2024 the Space Bureau acted on SpaceX's application to add mobile-satellite service to Gen2 in the Big LEO bands, the 2 GHz bands, and 2020-2025 MHz uplink. Was that application accepted for filing, was it held in abeyance while SpaceX's rulemaking petitions were pending, and what file number was dismissed?
reference:
DA-24-300. The application is ICFS File No. SAT-MOD-20230207-00022, filed 7 February 2023. It is not SAT-MOD-20230207-00021. That other file is the separate SCS modification.

The Bureau dismissed 00022 on its own motion as unacceptable for filing. It had not been accepted for filing and had not been placed on public notice. The 1.6/2.4 GHz and 2 GHz bands were not available for an additional MSS applicant. The leftover request, MSS uplink only in 2020-2025 MHz, is not a comprehensive proposal under section 25.114. In the United States that band is allocated to fixed and mobile, with no MSS allocation.

On 5 February 2024 SpaceX asked that the application be held in abeyance while it sought a rulemaking, and also asked for a freeze on other MSS applications, including Globalstar and Gamma. The Bureau denied the abeyance. SpaceX gained no rights by filing an application that was unacceptable when filed. The freeze request, as made in this application proceeding, is dismissed as beyond its scope. If the Commission later opens the bands, SpaceX may reapply. Until then this application cannot be processed.

The DISH petition to dismiss or deny, and SpaceX's motion to strike, are dismissed as moot because the application itself is dismissed.

Wrong: the Bureau parked 00022 until the rulemaking. Wrong: this is the same file as the T-Mobile SCS modification. A later dismissal with prejudice, in DA-26-398, is a different order and a different list of files.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-24-300A1.pdf

text: On 29 June 2026 SpaceX filed written representations with ICASA on the draft amendment of the Radio Frequency Spectrum Fees Regulations. Did that filing grant Starlink a South African spectrum licence, and for what term? What equity rule does SpaceX say the draft leaves unresolved?
reference:
SpaceX written representations to ICASA, 29 June 2026, on Notice 3926 of 2026, Government Gazette No. 54677, 15 May 2026. This document is a comment on a draft. It is not a spectrum licence and it does not grant one.

SpaceX says it intends to provide Starlink to South African consumers and businesses in future through its South African subsidiary. The draft, if final, would govern fees for gateway earth stations and user-terminal networks. That sentence is SpaceX's statement of intent. It is not an ICASA grant, and it is not a finding that every other authorisation is absent.

The draft does not set the duration of gateway or user-terminal network licences. SpaceX asks for a minimum term of 10 years, with renewal criteria and a timeline. Ten years is SpaceX's request, not a term ICASA granted on 29 June 2026.

SpaceX says the existing Radio Frequency Spectrum Regulations impose a minimum 30 percent Historically Disadvantaged Group equity requirement on applicants for and holders of radio frequency spectrum licences, and that the draft does not say how that requirement applies to the new gateway and user-terminal network categories. SpaceX asks the Authority to confirm it. The 12 December 2025 ministerial policy direction on aligning spectrum licensing with the ICT Sector Code is noted by SpaceX as a separate process the draft does not complete.

The satellite-licensing inquiry findings in Government Gazette 52530, General Notice 3144 of 2025, are findings on a framework. They are not this fee filing, and they are not a Starlink licence.

Wrong: ICASA licensed Starlink for 10 years on 29 June 2026. Wrong: the comment letter abolished the 30 percent equity rule.

Source: https://www.icasa.org.za/uploads/files/Space-X_Redacted.pdf

text: SpaceX was first authorized for a separate V-band constellation of up to 7,500 satellites. Did that separate constellation survive, and what did the 26 November 2024 order actually allow at 340 to 360 km? Was the later request to change the V-band bond and milestones already granted on that date?
reference:
SpaceX was originally authorized to operate up to 7,500 satellites as a separate V-band constellation. It later committed to put V-band on the Gen2 satellites instead. On 13 October 2023 the Space Bureau granted in part and dismissed in part SAT-MOD-20230322-00062, adding V-band to Gen2 rather than keeping the separate constellation. DA-24-222 paragraph 4 and DA-24-1193 footnote 34 state that.

DA-24-1193, 26 November 2024, grants the V-band modification so those previously authorized Gen2 satellites may use V-band at 340 km to 360 km. The frequencies recited for that earlier V-band grant are 37.5-40.0 GHz and 40.0-42.0 GHz space-to-Earth, and 47.2-50.2 GHz and 50.4-51.4 GHz Earth-to-space. This is not a new 7,500-satellite constellation on top of Gen2.

As of that 26 November 2024 order, SAT-MOD-20240813-00183, the request to modify the V-band bond and milestone conditions, remained pending. Do not treat it as granted on that date, and do not invent a later disposition.

Wrong: the separate V-band constellation is still authorized alongside Gen2. Wrong: the November 2024 order granted the bond and milestone change.

Sources: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-24-1193A1.pdf and https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-24-222A1.pdf

text: In 2018 the Commission dismissed SpaceX's request to operate in 51.4-52.4 GHz and deferred 50.4-51.4 GHz. Does the January 2026 Gen2 grant still exclude both of those uplinks?
reference:
FCC-18-161. The public notice accepting the V-band application had included 51.4-52.4 GHz in error. There was no international or domestic satellite allocation in that band, so the request to operate there was dismissed. The request to use 50.4-51.4 GHz for service and gateway uplinks was deferred, not granted, pending the Spectrum Frontiers proceeding, GN Docket 14-177. The request for 42.0-42.5 GHz was also dismissed in that order. The 2018 milestones and bond ran with that separate V-band authorization. Do not treat those 2018 milestone dates as the milestone dates of the January 2026 Gen2 grant.

DA-26-36, the 9 January 2026 Gen2 order, lists Earth-to-space uplinks at 47.2-50.2 GHz, 50.4-51.4 GHz, and 51.4-52.4 GHz on the Gen2 space-station grant. The 2018 dismissal does not still exclude those two uplinks from that later grant.

Wrong: both uplinks are still refused because of the 2018 order. Wrong: 50.4-51.4 GHz was granted in 2018.

Sources: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-18-161A1.txt and https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt

text: El decreto de 9 de enero de 2025 otorga a Starlink Chile SpA una concesión de servicio intermedio de telecomunicaciones. ¿Por cuántos años corre, desde qué fecha, y la banda 27,5-28,35 GHz autoriza cualquier estación terrena en la ciudad? ¿La publicación del 21 de marzo de 2026 en el Diario Oficial ya autorizó el gateway adicional?
reference:
Decreto del Ministerio de Transportes y Telecomunicaciones, Santiago, 9 de enero de 2025, identificado en la Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional como Decreto 5. Otorga a Starlink Chile SpA, RUT 77.073.851-2, una concesión de Servicio Intermedio de Telecomunicaciones para instalar, operar y explotar siete estaciones terrenas conectadas a la constelación Starlink, en bandas del servicio fijo por satélite.

La vigencia es de 30 años contados desde la publicación en el Diario Oficial del decreto que la autoriza. No corre desde el 9 de enero de 2025 por el solo hecho de la fecha del decreto. No inventar el día de esa publicación si el texto no lo fija como inicio distinto de la publicación.

Según el Plan General de Uso del Espectro, en 27,5-28,35 GHz (Tierra-espacio) solo se autorizan estaciones terrenas de pasarela. Deben estar fuera de zonas urbanas consolidadas y no causar interferencias perjudiciales a los servicios fijos o móviles en zonas urbanas consolidadas o industriales que se autoricen al amparo de la resolución exenta 836 de 2020.

La concesionaria debe informar, dentro de los primeros 5 días hábiles de febrero, junio y octubre, el número de estaciones en el sistema hasta el último día hábil del mes anterior. Si no informa, la Subsecretaría cobra con los antecedentes de que disponga.

El extracto 25-SP69681, Diario Oficial del 21 de marzo de 2026, no es el decreto que autoriza la modificación. Es la publicación, bajo el artículo 15 de la ley 18.168, de una solicitud para modificar el decreto supremo 156 de 2021 y agregar una estación terrena gateway. Quien tenga interés puede oponerse dentro de 30 días hábiles desde esa publicación. Los plazos de 1, 22 y 24 meses que el extracto menciona corren desde la publicación en el Diario Oficial del decreto que autorice la modificación, no desde el 21 de marzo de 2026.

Falso: la banda 27,5-28,35 GHz autoriza terminales de usuario dentro de la ciudad. Falso: el Diario Oficial del 21 de marzo de 2026 ya otorgó el gateway nuevo.

Fuentes: https://www.bcn.cl/leychile/navegar?idNorma=1211378 y https://www.subtel.gob.cl/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Solicitud-numero-25-SP69681.-Starlink-Chile-SpA.pdf

text: On 1 December 2022 the Commission partially granted the Gen2 application and authorized 7,500 satellites. Did that increase the number of satellites SpaceX was allowed to have on orbit, and were E-band and the tracking beacons included?
reference:
FCC-22-91, released 1 December 2022, IBFS File Nos. SAT-LOA-20200526-00055 and SAT-AMD-20210818-00105. SpaceX had asked for 29,988 Gen2 satellites. The order grants 7,500, at 525 km and 53 degrees, 530 km and 43 degrees, and 535 km and 33 degrees, in Ku and Ka band. It defers the rest of the application, including E-band and the tracking beacons. It does not grant E-band.

Paragraph 2 states that the grant does not increase the total number of satellites SpaceX is authorized to deploy, and in fact slightly reduces it, compared with what SpaceX might otherwise have deployed. The reason given is SpaceX's commitment to modify the earlier V-band license so those V-band operations fold into Gen2 instead of flying as a separate system. The later 13 October 2023 stamp is the modification that carried out that commitment. It is not this order.

The same order recalls that Gen1, 4,425 satellites, was granted on 28 March 2018. As of this order, the D.C. Circuit had upheld the third Gen1 modification on 26 August 2022, and petitions for reconsideration of that third modification were still pending. Do not treat those petitions as resolved by FCC-22-91.

Wrong: December 2022 added 7,500 satellites on top of every existing authorization. Wrong: E-band and the beacons were granted that day.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-22-91A1.pdf

text: The 1 December 2022 Gen2 partial grant put the 7,500 satellites at 525, 530, and 535 km. Did that order let one of those satellites use two co-frequency beams on the same area, and did it let them operate at or above 580 km?
reference:
FCC-22-91, adopted 29 November 2022, released 1 December 2022, call sign S3069. Paragraph 2 conditions the partial grant, for operations in certain frequency bands, on using no more than one satellite beam from any authorized Gen2 satellite in the same frequency in the same or overlapping areas at a time. It also limits operations to below 580 km. The granted shells in that order are 525 km at 53 degrees, 530 km at 43 degrees, and 535 km at 33 degrees.

The one-beam limit is for certain frequency bands, not a sentence that names every band. Do not invent a later removal of the condition, and do not invent an eight-beam substitute, unless the answer is separately citing a later order for that later change. This question is about FCC-22-91.

Wrong: each satellite could light two co-frequency beams on the same area. Wrong: 580 km was a floor.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-22-91A1.txt

text: La décision Arcep n° 2022-1102 du 25 mai 2022 autorisait-elle déjà les stations terriennes en mouvement? Quelle décision a ajouté les ESIM, pour quel seul système UIT, et quelle PIRE maximale leur est imposée?
reference:
Décision n° 2023-0680 du 28 mars 2023, qui modifie la décision n° 2022-1102 du 25 mai 2022.

La décision de mai 2022, telle que la décision de 2023 la rappelle, autorisait des stations terriennes fixes chez des clients résidentiels, avec STEAM-1, dans 10,95-12,70 GHz espace vers Terre et 14,0-14,50 GHz Terre vers espace. Elle n'autorisait pas les ESIM.

La décision 2023-0680 autorise les liaisons avec STEAM-1 seulement, vers des stations fixes et des ESIM, dans 10,70-12,75 GHz espace vers Terre et 14,00-14,50 GHz Terre vers espace, sur le territoire dont l'Arcep est affectataire. Sans garantie de non-brouillage, et avec une obligation de non-interférence. La PIRE maximale des ESIM est 54,5 dBW, selon ECC/DEC/(18)05. STEAM-1B et USASAT-NGSO-3X ne sont pas dans cette décision. Ils relèvent d'une décision postérieure.

La consultation citée dans les visas va du 12 juillet 2022 au 22 septembre 2022. Les motifs disent du 21 juillet au 22 septembre 2022. Ne pas trancher cette différence de date comme si un seul jour était certain.

Faux: les ESIM étaient déjà dans la décision du 25 mai 2022. Faux: la décision du 28 mars 2023 autorise STEAM-1B. Ne pas noter 60 dBW: ce chiffre n'est pas la PIRE ESIM de cette décision.

Source: https://www.arcep.fr/uploads/tx_gsavis/23-0680.pdf

text: Heeft de RDI in 2025 aan SpaceX Netherlands B.V. een concessie verleend voor heel Nederland? Wat gebood de inspectie in juni 2024, waarom werd de aanvraag van 26 juni 2024 afgewezen, en welke vennootschap kreeg daarna voor welke eilanden en voor hoe lang een concessie?
reference:
Nota van de RDI in het Woo-besluit van 20 januari 2026, en het nieuwsbericht van de RDI van 1 december 2025. Dit gaat over Caribisch Nederland, niet over Europees Nederland. Deze stukken verlenen geen concessie voor Europees Nederland en wijzen die ook niet af.

Eind 2023 signaleerde een lokale aanbieder dat Starlink zonder concessie internetdiensten aanbood in Caribisch Nederland. De RDI stelde vast dat dat ongeoorloofd was. Op 14 juni 2024 sommeerde de RDI SpaceX de diensten uiterlijk 21 juni 2024 te staken. SpaceX gaf daaraan geen gehoor. Op 5 augustus 2024 volgde een tweede sommatie om per 7 augustus te staken. Daaraan gaf SpaceX wel gehoor. Het toezichtstraject is daarmee afgesloten.

Op 26 juni 2024 diende SpaceX Netherlands B.V. een concessieaanvraag in. Het Besluit radio-elektrische inrichtingen BES eist een inschrijving in het handelsregister van de Kamer van Koophandel en Fabrieken BES, dus een lokale entiteit. Op 11 juli 2024 is SpaceX daarop gewezen. Op 7 februari 2025 is die aanvraag afgewezen omdat de inschrijving ontbrak. Die afwijzing is geen verlening.

Op 23 juli 2025 vroeg Starlink Caribbean LLC, handelsnaam Starlink Bonaire, handelsregisternummer 15854, een concessie voor Bonaire, Saba en Sint Eustatius. Die aanvraag voldeed aan de inschrijving. Het nieuwsbericht van de RDI van 1 december 2025 zegt dat de concessie is verleend voor satellietcommunicatiediensten op Bonaire, Sint Eustatius en Saba, voor vijftien jaar. De concessie is voor openbare telecommunicatie-infrastructuur. Artikel 43 van de Wet telecommunicatievoorzieningen BES verplicht de concessiehouder mee te werken aan een last tot aftappen of opnemen.

Fout: SpaceX Netherlands B.V. kreeg in februari 2025 een concessie voor heel Nederland. Fout: de concessie van december 2025 is verleend aan dezelfde vennootschap als de afgewezen aanvraag. Fout: de eerste sommatie van 14 juni 2024 werd meteen nageleefd.

Bronnen: https://www.rdi.nl/actueel/nieuws/2025/12/01/rdi-grants-concession-contract-to-starlink-for-satellite-services-on-bonaire-sint-eustatius-and-saba en https://open.overheid.nl/documenten/65ac8267-005d-4692-bedf-f5cbc5f108d6/file

text: The December 2022 Gen2 grant required SpaceX to coordinate with earlier NGSO systems and to make a specific report about the ITU's EPFD finding. Does a favorable finding on one Gen2 ITU filing satisfy that report, and may SpaceX keep deploying if satellite failures exceed the threshold in the order?
reference:
FCC-22-91, released 1 December 2022, paragraph 2.

SpaceX must report whether the ITU finding on compliance with EPFD limits takes into account all of the relevant ITU filings for the Gen2 system combined. A favorable or qualified-favorable finding on a single filing is not, by itself, that report. The order also conditions the grant on coordination with NGSO FSS systems licensed in certain prior processing rounds. It does not name those systems in the introductory paragraph. Do not invent the list.

The same paragraph requires SpaceX to pause deployment of new satellites if satellite failures exceed the threshold set in the order. It does not allow deployment to continue through that threshold. This introductory paragraph does not state the numeric threshold. Do not invent the percentage or the count. The obligation to pause is the graded holding.

The same paragraph requires SpaceX to report mitigation actions taken to avoid collisions, and to coordinate with NASA on launch windows. It requires coordination with the National Science Foundation and with specific observatories for radio astronomy. Do not invent which observatories if the answer is relying only on this paragraph.

Wrong: any one favorable ITU finding closes the reporting condition. Wrong: SpaceX may keep launching new Gen2 satellites after the failure threshold is crossed.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-22-91A1.txt

text: In early March 2026 the FCC acted on several SpaceX Services earth-station files. Were those actions ordinary licenses still in force on 8 October 2026? For the special temporary authorities with an end date, what basis were they granted on, when did the term end, and which two actions that same week were instead continuing-operations grants under section 1.62?
reference:
Public notice text in DOC-419216A1. These are not new full-term earth-station licenses. Do not invent a renewal after the printed end date.

Granted on an unprotected and non-interference basis, and only within the parameters requested, with the licensee still bound by the space-station grant for the associated points of communication:

SES-STA-20260109-00645, call sign E230070, filed 9 January 2026, term 3 March 2026 through 1 May 2026, action 3 March 2026.
SES-STA-20260109-00642, E230106, filed 12 January 2026, term 3 March 2026 through 1 May 2026, action 3 March 2026.
SES-STA-20260109-00640, E220075, filed 12 January 2026, term 3 March 2026 through 1 May 2026, action 3 March 2026.
SES-STA-20260109-00625, E230147, filed 12 January 2026, term 27 February 2026 through 27 April 2026, action 26 February 2026.
SES-STA-20260211-00685, E210127, filed 12 February 2026, term 3 March 2026 through 1 April 2026, action 3 March 2026.
SES-STA-20260211-00687, E210309, filed 12 February 2026, term 3 March 2026 through 1 April 2026, action 3 March 2026.

On 8 October 2026 every one of those printed terms is over.

Two different actions the same week are not those dated STAs. SES-STA-20260117-00812, E220009, action 2 March 2026, and SES-STA-20260117-00918, E210309, action 2 March 2026, were granted pursuant to section 1.62 to reflect continuing operations. The public notice does not put an end date on those two. E210309 therefore has both a 1.62 continuing-operations action and a separate STA, file 00687, that ended 1 April 2026. Do not treat those as the same grant.

Wrong: the March 2026 actions were ordinary licenses still running in October. Wrong: the two section 1.62 actions expired on 1 May 2026.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-419216A1.txt

text: New Zealand decided in 2026 how 27.5-28.35 GHz would be shared between mobile and fixed-satellite gateways. Do satellite gateways get that band inside cities on the same footing as mobile? When could an existing interim gateway apply for a long-term licence, and when did applications for a new gateway open?
reference:
Radio Spectrum Management, Future use of the 24-30 GHz spectrum, and the RSM news item of 7 April 2026. This is the allocation and licensing rule. It is not a grant of a Starlink licence, and it does not name Starlink. Do not invent a Starlink call sign or a New Zealand expiry for a Starlink station.

In 27.5-28.35 GHz the Government adopted geographic sharing: mobile inside urban areas, fixed-satellite service outside urban areas. There is a limited, time-bound application window for new satellite gateways that already had plans in urban areas. After that period, MBIE accepts satellite licence requests only outside urban areas. A gateway does not get the urban band on the same footing as mobile.

Long-term applications for existing earth stations in 27.5-30 GHz, as defined in the licensing rules, were accepted until 22 May 2026. During that period other licensing in the band was paused so existing licences could be processed ahead of expiry. The 7 April 2026 news says applications for fixed-satellite gateways already operating under interim licences opened on 2 April 2026.

Applications for new gateways, feeder links, and user terminals or VSAT earth stations could be submitted from 09:00 on 8 June 2026. The news says licensing for new fixed-satellite gateways was expected to open on 8 June 2026. 2 April 2026 is not the opening date for a new gateway.

Wrong: satellite gateways and mobile share 27.5-28.35 GHz inside cities without a geographic split. Wrong: a new gateway application could be filed on 2 April 2026.

Sources: https://www.rsm.govt.nz/projects-and-auctions/current-projects/future-use-of-the-24-30-ghz-spectrum and https://www.rsm.govt.nz/about/news-and-updates/24-30-ghz-public-consultation-outcomes-and-radio-licensing-open-for-some-services

text: Section 25.146 required a favorable or qualified-favorable ITU finding on EPFD limits before an NGSO system could start operating. Did the 1 December 2022 Gen2 partial grant make SpaceX wait for that finding, and did the waiver erase the conditions in the same order?
reference:
FCC-22-91, ordering clause 141, as printed in the FCC Record. The request for a waiver of the requirement to receive a favorable or qualified-favorable finding, in accordance with Resolution 85 (WRC-03), on compliance with the equivalent power-flux-density limits in Article 22 of the ITU Radio Regulations, before commencing operations, is GRANTED, subject to the conditions set forth above.

The ordering clause as reprinted cites that requirement under 47 CFR 25.146(a). Footnote 48 of the discussion identifies the rule SpaceX asked to waive as 47 CFR 25.146(c). That citation difference is not a second waiver. Do not grade ordering clause 140. The extract of that clause, on the Ka-band PFD waiver of section 25.146(a)(1), is incomplete.

The waiver does not delete Article 22, and it does not erase the conditions earlier in the order. Those conditions include the requirement to report whether the ITU EPFD finding takes into account all relevant Gen2 ITU filings combined. A waiver of the prior-finding gate is not a finding that the limits were met.

Wrong: SpaceX had to wait for the ITU finding before it could commence the operations authorized on 1 December 2022. Wrong: the waiver removed the combined-filings report.

Sources: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-22-91A1.pdf and the FCC Record reprint at https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc2303643/m1/1030/

text: Under the Communications Authority of Kenya's telecommunications market-structure review, may a foreign satellite operator keep delivering cross-border connectivity to Kenyan networks with no landing-rights authorization? From when does the transitional note say applications for the new categories are made, and does that note grant Starlink one?
reference:
Communications Authority of Kenya, Transitional Provisions, Telecommunication Market Structure Review, 2025, and the Authority's market-structure page.

Foreign firms that currently provide, or intend to provide, satellite or terrestrial cross-border connectivity to in-country infrastructure providers will be required to apply for a Landing Rights Authorization. An operator already providing that connectivity is in the class that must apply. The note does not grandfather current satellite service in place of the authorization.

The transitional table places applications for the new licence categories, including LRA, after 1 November 2025, and upon development of the licences for those categories. That date is the start of the application window described in the table. It is not, in this document, an order that service stop on that day.

Landing Rights Authorization is its own category. The market-structure page, describing the structure established in April 2026, lists it under international infrastructure and service licences, separate from an international gateway licence. The transitional note does not grant Starlink a landing-rights authorization, and it does not refuse one. Do not invent a Starlink Kenya licence number or a suspension.

Wrong: a foreign satellite firm already serving Kenyan networks was excused from landing rights. Wrong: the 2025 note is Starlink's Kenyan licence.

Sources: https://ca.go.ke/sites/default/files/2025-09/Transitional%20Provisions%20-%20Telecommunication%20Market%20Structure%20Review%20-%202025%20.pdf and https://www.ca.go.ke/market-structure

text: The Nigerian Communications Commission register lists SpaceX against 6,000 satellites and an end date of 31 December 2028. Is that landing permit a licence for 6,000 satellites running as long as Starlink's Nigerian gateway licences, and is the Ka-band uplink a continuous 27.5-30 GHz block?
reference:
Nigerian Communications Commission, authorized space-services operators register. Dates on that register are day/month/year. 31/12/2028 is 31 December 2028.

The SpaceX row is a landing permit, notifying administration Norway, for the STEAM-1, STEAM-2 and STEAM-2B constellation, NGSO LEO, fixed-satellite service. The register's own note says the Commission authorized the full constellation of 4,408 satellites and issued a landing permit of seven years for the 3,594 satellites launched at the time of the application. Signals may be beamed over Nigeria until December 2028. The permit is subject to review and extension pending launch of the full 4,408. A column on the same row shows 6,000. Those are three different figures. The landing permit described in the note is for the 3,594 then launched, not for 6,000, and it is not a grant of the full 4,408 without the stated review.

The row is dated 7 January 2021, duration shown as 7 years, end date 31 December 2028. Grade the end date the register prints. Do not replace it with 7 January 2028 by adding seven years yourself.

Frequencies on that row: Earth-to-space 27.5-29.1 GHz and 29.5-30.0 GHz, so not a continuous 27.5-30 GHz uplink. Space-to-Earth 17.8-18.6 GHz and 18.8-19.3 GHz. Earth-to-space 14.0-14.5 GHz. Space-to-Earth 10.7-12.7 GHz.

Separate rows, not this landing permit, licence Starlink Internet Services Nigeria Limited: five Ka-band gateway earth stations, at Tarau, Ibeju Lekki, Ikire, Sakpenwa, and Murfa, Kalam, each 4 July 2022 to 4 July 2032. A Ku-band VSAT authorization, nationwide, 28 June 2022 to 27 June 2032. Those 2032 dates are not the landing permit. A further nationwide Ku-band VSAT row for Africa Mobile Network Communications Ltd, 1 May 2024 to 1 May 2034, names the Starlink constellation and is not Starlink Internet Services Nigeria Limited.

Wrong: the landing permit is 6,000 satellites through 2032. Wrong: the Ka uplink is continuous from 27.5 to 30 GHz.

Source: https://www.ncc.gov.ng/authorized-space-services-operators

text: SpaceX's Gen2 application proposed tracking beacons in the 137-138 MHz and 148-150.05 MHz bands. Did the 1 December 2022 partial grant authorize those beacons, and which direction did the application assign to each band?
reference:
FCC-22-91, paragraphs 1 and 8. The application proposes tracking beacons communicating in 137.00-138.00 MHz Earth-to-space and 148.00-150.05 MHz space-to-Earth. The 137 MHz band is the uplink in that proposal. The 148 MHz band is the downlink.

Paragraph 1 defers consideration of the proposed E-band frequencies and of the tracking beacons. The partial grant does not authorize the beacons. Authority to conduct telemetry, tracking, and command while removing satellites from orbit, consistent with the application, is a different grant. It is not an authorization of these VHF beacons.

A later order, in November 2024, is where beacons were addressed again. Do not treat that later grant as the 1 December 2022 order, and do not move these two bands onto that later beacon authorization unless that later order says so.

Wrong: the December 2022 grant authorized the beacons. Wrong: the application put 137-138 MHz on the space-to-Earth link.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-22-91A1.txt

text: In October 2025 the FAA adopted the environmental impact statement for Falcon launches at Vandenberg and selected redevelopment of SLC-6 plus a higher cadence at SLC-4. Did that record of decision issue the license, and what still has to be satisfied before a license for those operations can be granted?
reference:
FAA Record of Decision, October 2025, adopting the Environmental Impact Statement for changes to the Falcon launch program at Vandenberg Space Force Base. The Department of the Air Force was the lead agency. The FAA and the Coast Guard were cooperating agencies.

The FAA concurs with and adopts the EIS analysis. Its federal action would be issuance or modification of a license for Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy operations, to increase the annual launch and landing cadence at SLC-4 and to establish Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy operations at SLC-6, plus associated temporary airspace closures, and potential renewals and modifications inside the scope of the EIS.

The record of decision is not that license. The document says completion of the environmental review does not guarantee that the FAA will issue a license for Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy operations at SLC-4 and SLC-6. text: The FAA's commercial-space waiver notice, docket FAA-2026-8614, lists the National Environmental Policy Act among laws to be waived for launch licenses. Has that notice already waived NEPA for a Falcon license?
reference:
FAA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Notice No. 26-11, RIN 2120-AM51, Docket No. FAA-2026-8614. It proposes to amend 14 CFR parts 400, 420, 433, 437, and 450. It is not a final rule. The comment date in the notice text is a publication placeholder. Do not invent a Federal Register effective date.

FAA Record of Decision, October 2025, adopting the environmental impact statement for changes to the Falcon launch program at Vandenberg Space Force Base.

text: After the insurance policy on a licensed Falcon launch expires, does the United States still pay only the layer above that policy? And did the rule that names a space flight participant as an additional insured expire on 30 September 2025?
reference:
14 CFR part 440 and 51 USC 50914, 2024 edition, as amended by Public Law 118-159.

While the policy is in force, third-party claims for a licensed activity that exceed the insurance required under 440.9(c), and that do not exceed $1,500,000,000 above that insurance, as adjusted for inflation after 1 January 1989, are payable under 51 USC 50915 and 14 CFR 440.19. That layer starts above the required insurance. It is not first-dollar coverage.

After the policy period in 14 CFR 440.11(a) expires, the United States provides for payment of claims payable under 51 USC 50915 from the first dollar of loss, up to $1,500,000,000 as adjusted for inflation after 1 January 1989. The post-policy payment is not the same layer as the payment during the policy.

For purposes of part 440, a space flight participant is not a customer.

14 CFR 440.9(b)(4), the additional-insured requirement for space flight participants, and 14 CFR 440.17(f), the licensee-participant reciprocal waiver, each say they cease to be effective on 30 September 2025 unless public law modifies the limitation in 51 USC 50914.

51 USC 50914(a)(4)(E) includes space flight participants among the persons the insurance must protect. Subsection (a)(5) says that subparagraph ceases to be effective on 30 September 2028. Subsection (b)(1) makes space flight participants applicable parties to the statutory reciprocal waiver, and (b)(1)(C) says that clause ceases to be effective on 30 September 2028. The 2024 code notes that Public Law 118-159 replaced 30 September 2025 with 30 September 2028 in both places. The CFR's printed 2025 date is the date that governs only if Congress had not modified 50914. Congress did modify those two dates.

Wrong: after the policy expires the government still pays only above the old insurance limit. Wrong: participant additional-insured status ended on 30 September 2025 because the CFR still prints that date. Do not invent the inflation-adjusted dollar amount. The texts state the $1,500,000,000 base and the adjustment. They do not compute it.

Sources: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-440 and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title51/html/USCODE-2024-title51-subtitleV-chap509-sec50914.htm

text: If third-party claims from a licensed Falcon launch exceed the required insurance, does the United States automatically pay the next $1.5 billion? Does that statute cover an experimental permit, or a loss caused by the licensee's willful misconduct?
reference:
51 USC 50915, text in effect on 15 May 2026. The Secretary of Transportation provides for payment of a successful third-party claim only to the extent provided in advance in an appropriation law, or to the extent additional legislative authority is enacted for a compensation plan submitted under subsection (d). It is not an automatic payment.

Payment is only for the amount of successful claims from one launch or reentry that is more than the insurance or demonstration of financial responsibility required under 50914(a)(1)(A), and not more than $1,500,000,000, plus amounts necessary to reflect inflation after 1 January 1989, above that insurance. Do not compute the inflation-adjusted dollar figure. The statute states the base and the adjustment. It does not multiply it out.

The Secretary may not pay a part of a claim for death, bodily injury, or property damage that results from willful misconduct by the licensee or transferee. If a usual policy exclusion, as the Secretary decides that phrase, leaves a successful third-party claim uninsured, the Secretary may pay the excluded claim without regard to the limitation in 50914(a)(1).

Before a payment: the government must be notified of the claim or the civil action, the government must be given an opportunity to assist in the defense, and the Secretary must approve any part of a settlement to be paid from government appropriations. The Secretary may withhold a payment certified as not reasonable. An amount finally decided by a court of competent jurisdiction is deemed reasonable.

If a court determination indicates that liability for one launch or reentry may exceed the required insurance, the President, on the Secretary's recommendation, submits a compensation plan to Congress not later than 90 days after that determination. For a single event or incident, that plan may not be for more than $1,500,000,000. That sentence does not repeat the inflation adjustment stated in subsection (a).

Subsection (f): this section applies to a license issued or transferred under the chapter for which the Secretary receives a complete and valid application not later than 30 September 2028. It does not apply to permits.

Wrong: the $1.5 billion is paid automatically once claims exceed the insurance. Wrong: an experimental permit gets the same payment. Wrong: willful misconduct by the licensee is covered.

Source: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title51-section50915&num=0&edition=prelim

text: A space flight participant, or a third party, wants to sue in state court for injury from a licensed Falcon launch. Does federal law allow that forum, and does the same sentence cover an experimental permit?
reference:
51 USC 50914(g). Any claim by a third party or a space flight participant for death, bodily injury, or property damage or loss resulting from an activity carried out under the license is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal courts.

A state-court forum clause does not move that claim. The sentence covers a third party and a space flight participant. It does not, in this subsection, name a crew member as a separate category. It says the activity is carried out under the license. It does not say an experimental permit. Do not extend the sentence to a permit.

Wrong: the participant may sue in state court. Wrong: subsection (g) is the permit rule as well as the license rule.

Source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title51/html/USCODE-2024-title51-subtitleV-chap509-sec50914.htm

text: A suborbital licensed flight is insured on the same clock as an orbital launch: coverage runs until 30 days after payload separation. Is that the rule, and when does the coverage attach?
reference:
14 CFR 440.11. Insurance required under 440.9, or another form of financial responsibility, attaches when a licensed launch or permitted activity starts. It does not attach when the policy is merely bound.

It remains in force until completion of the licensed launch or permitted activities at a launch or reentry site.

For an orbital launch, it also remains in force until the later of 30 days after payload separation, or attempted payload separation if separation is anomalous, and 30 days from ignition of the launch vehicle.

A suborbital launch does not use that 30-day clock. Coverage remains until the later of motor impact and payload recovery, or the FAA's determination that the risk to third parties and government property from the licensed launch or permitted activity is small enough that financial responsibility is no longer necessary. That determination is made in the risk analysis conducted before launch to determine maximum probable loss, and it is specified in a license or permit order.

Financial responsibility may not be replaced, cancelled, changed, withdrawn, or otherwise modified to reduce the limits or the extent of coverage, and it may not expire by its own terms, before the time specified in a license or permit order, unless the FAA is notified at least 30 days in advance and expressly approves the modification.

Wrong: a suborbital flight is insured until 30 days after payload separation. Wrong: coverage attaches when the policy is issued, even if the launch has not started.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-440/subpart-A/section-440.11

text: Is every property-damage claim by the United States on a licensed launch paid from the $100 million government-property cover? If the operator shows financial responsibility without buying a policy, when is that evidence due, and is a certificate of insurance enough on its own?
reference:
14 CFR 440.9 and 440.15.

A condition of each license or permit is to meet the insurance requirements, or otherwise to demonstrate the required amount of financial responsibility.

Under 440.9(c), the third-party amount is based on maximum probable loss and will not exceed the lesser of $500 million or the maximum liability insurance available on the world market at a reasonable cost, as determined by the FAA. A covered third-party claim includes a claim by the United States, its agencies, and its contractors and subcontractors for damage or loss to property other than property for which insurance is required under paragraph (d). A government claim for that other property is in the third-party bucket. It is not automatically the paragraph (d) cover.

Paragraph (e) sets the amount for property damage under paragraph (d). That amount is based on maximum probable loss and will not exceed the lesser of $100 million or the maximum available on the world market at a reasonable cost, as determined by the FAA.

Under 440.9(f), instead of a policy the licensee or permittee may demonstrate financial responsibility another way that meets the terms and conditions for insurance in this part. It must describe the method in detail and how the method covers the claims.

Evidence of insurance is due at least 30 days before a licensed launch or permitted activity, and for a licensed reentry no less than 30 days before launch activities involving the reentry licensee, unless the Administrator agrees to another time under 404.15. Evidence of financial responsibility in a form other than insurance, under 440.9(f), is due at least 60 days before the licensed or permitted activity, unless the Administrator agrees to another time. The 30-day insurance clock is not the clock for a non-insurance demonstration.

Proof of insurance includes a certificate of insurance, signed by the insurer, showing a currently effective and properly endorsed policy, the terms and amounts, and the exclusions. The certificate must be accompanied by an opinion of the insurance broker that the insurance complies with this part and any applicable license or permit order. The certificate alone is not that proof.

Wrong: every United States property claim is inside the $100 million cover. Wrong: an escrow or other non-insurance demonstration is due on the 30-day insurance schedule. Wrong: the insurer's certificate, without the broker's opinion, is the required proof.

Sources: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-440/subpart-A/section-440.9 and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-440/subpart-A/section-440.15

text: Does the insurance on a launch license protect only the licensee? Does a customer's contractor have to pay the United States for its own cover?
reference:
51 USC 50914(a)(4), 2024 edition. When a launch or reentry license is issued or transferred, the licensee or transferee must obtain liability insurance or demonstrate financial responsibility. The policy or demonstration under subsection (a) must protect the following, to the extent of their potential liability for involvement in launch services or reentry services, at no cost to the Government:

(A) the Government.
(B) executive agencies and personnel, contractors, and subcontractors of the Government.
(C) contractors, subcontractors, and customers of the licensee or transferee.
(D) contractors and subcontractors of the customer.

A customer's contractor is on that list. The protection is at no cost to the Government. The statute does not require that contractor to buy a separate policy from the United States. The printed list does not add a separate line for a space flight participant.

text: Did the FAA's finding on a higher Starship cadence at Boca Chica license 25 launches a year, including night landings back at the pad?
reference:
FAA Mitigated Finding of No Significant Impact and Record of Decision for the Final Tiered Environmental Assessment of a higher Starship/Super Heavy cadence at Boca Chica, issued in April 2025. This document is tiered from the June 2022 programmatic assessment. It is not license VOL 23-129 and it is not the April 2023 order.

The FAA determined that modifying VOL 23-129 to support the higher cadence would not significantly affect the quality of the human environment within the meaning of NEPA. An environmental impact statement is not required. The final tiered assessment is incorporated by reference. That determination is not the issuance of the modified license.

SpaceX's proposed action is up to 25 launches a year and 50 landings a year, 25 of Starship and 25 of Super Heavy, plus vehicle and operational upgrades. Up to three of those 25 launches would be at night from the vertical launch area. Landings at the vertical launch area would be in daytime only, up to 22 Starship and 22 Super Heavy. Daytime landings of either vehicle may also be offshore. Up to three Starship landings and three Super Heavy landings may be at night, and only offshore. Licensed daytime static-fire testing is capped at 90 seconds a year for Starship and 70 seconds a year for Super Heavy. Those are durations, not a count of tests.

The FAA's federal action is to modify the existing vehicle operator license for that cadence, including potential renewals and modifications inside the scope of the assessment, and to issue temporary airspace closures.

Under the no-action alternative the FAA would not modify a license for the higher cadence. Existing licenses would still allow up to five Starship launches and five Starship/Super Heavy launches a year, up to ten Starship landings, and up to five Super Heavy landings. No action is not a ban.

SpaceX must tell the FAA's Operational Safety Directorate, Safety Assurance Division, within 15 calendar days of a change to a representation in the license application, or in a document the FAA relied on, for the Boca Chica Starship/Super Heavy license. If a federal, state, or local environmental regulator alleges a violation in an investigative report, an administrative order, or a notice of violation, SpaceX must give the FAA copies within the time that regulator gave SpaceX to respond, or within 15 calendar days, whichever is shorter. If a Boca Chica launch is scheduled within 15 days after SpaceX receives such a notice, the notice to the FAA must be immediate and in writing.

Wrong: this finding is a license for 25 launches. Wrong: the pad is authorized for night landings. Wrong: the no-action case allows no flights.

text: Does the April 2025 finding on a higher Starship cadence let Boca Chica beach stay closed for as long as the launch campaign needs, including summer weekends?
reference:
The same April 2025 mitigated finding of no significant impact and record of decision as the cadence question. It is not the license.

Beach access restrictions continue under the memorandum of agreement between Cameron County and the Texas General Land Office, and only when necessary for public safety. They are limited to 500 hours a year for operations plus 300 hours a year for anomalies. The finding does not add anomaly hours beyond the 300 analyzed in the 2022 programmatic assessment. The total duration of access restrictions would not exceed 500 hours annually.

SpaceX has been not restricting access on holidays and weekends during summer months, as the 2022 assessment required. A year-round or summer-weekend closure is not what this finding allows.

On section 4(f), the proposed action would not permanently incorporate any section 4(f) property and would not cause a constructive use from visual effects, access limits, noise, or vibration. An anomaly could temporarily occupy some historic properties, Boca Chica State Park, and Brazos Island State Park. Those impacts are expected to be de minimis, and the FAA had concurrence from the officials with jurisdiction, including the Texas Historical Commission, Texas Parks and Wildlife, the Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Texas General Land Office. SpaceX continues the measures in the memorandum of agreement with Texas Parks and Wildlife for Boca Chica State Park, Brazos Island State Park, and other department land, and notifies the General Land Office of anomalies as appropriate.

text: Did the later Boca Chica airspace study authorize Starship to land back at the pad at night, and is the closed airspace only over the Gulf?
reference:
FAA final tiered environmental assessment of additional Starship-Super Heavy launch trajectories and Starship return-to-launch-site profiles at Boca Chica. SpaceX is seeking a modification of the existing vehicle operator license. This assessment studies that request. It is not the license, and it is not the April 2025 cadence finding. It is tiered from the 2022 programmatic assessment and from the April 2025 cadence assessment. Do not invent this document's signature date.

Daytime in the assumptions carried forward is 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. Night is 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. No Starship reentry at the Boca Chica launch site would occur at night. The three nighttime Starship reentries would be expended in the Gulf of America. No Super Heavy landing at the Boca Chica launch site would occur at night. Nighttime Super Heavy landings are assumed in the Gulf of America. The study uses the April 2025 assumption of up to 22 Starship reentries in daytime.

A Florida-overflight aircraft hazard area for launch and for Super Heavy landing could affect as few as 10 commercial aircraft an hour in the midnight period, and as many as 200 an hour in peak travel. Starship return-to-launch-site hazard areas could affect up to 200 commercial aircraft an hour in peak daytime, and up to 4,400 flights a year. The closed airspace is not a Gulf-only box.

Temporary closures are determined at least 72 hours before the launch or reentry, and the notice to airmen is issued after that determination. The hazard area can shrink as the vehicle becomes more reliable and empirical data accumulate. Its location and size vary by mission.

This assessment does not reanalyze biological resources, cultural resources, or section 4(f). Those categories stay with the earlier assessments.
