Source: https://www.faa.gov/space/stakeholder_engagement/spacex_starship/Final_Tiered_EA_Additional_Launch_Trajectories_Starship_RTLS_mission_profiles_SpaceX_Starship-Super_Heavy_Boca_Chica.pdf

text: Does a favorable FAA determination for the communications-satellite class clear every satellite on the next launch, including the parts the FCC regulates?
reference:
14 CFR 450.43. A favorable payload determination, when one is required, issues only if the applicant, payload owner, or payload operator has obtained all required licenses, authorizations, and permits, and the launch or reentry would not jeopardize public health and safety, safety of property, US national security or foreign policy interests, or international obligations of the United States.

An FCC license is not an FAA payload determination, and an FAA determination does not re-decide the FCC-regulated aspects.

The FAA may review a class of payload, including communications, remote sensing, or navigation. Before a launch or reentry, each payload is still subject to FAA verification that its launch or reentry would not jeopardize public health and safety, safety of property, national security or foreign policy interests, or international obligations. A class finding is not a clearance of every satellite in the class.

If an issue would impede a license, the FAA advises the requester in writing. The requester may respond in writing or amend the application under 413.17. A denial is in writing, states the reasons, and may be reviewed under 413.21.

A favorable determination for a payload or a class may be put into a license application. A change in the information required for the review must be reported under 413.17. The FAA decides whether the determination is still valid and may review the payload again.

text: Crew training is an allowed use of an experimental permit. Can the permittee charge a passenger for the flight, or fly a customer's payload for a fee?
reference:
14 CFR 437.5 and 437.91. An experimental permit may be issued to launch or reenter a reusable suborbital vehicle for crew training, for research and development, or for showing compliance with the requirements for a license. Section 437.91 is separate. No permittee may carry any property or human being for compensation or hire on a reusable suborbital vehicle.

Sources: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-437/subpart-A and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-437/subpart-D/section-437.91

text: DA-26-36, released 9 January 2026, grants SpaceX's request to remove the condition that limited operations to one co-frequency, co-polarization beam in any given location in the 12.2-12.7 GHz and 19.7-20.2 GHz bands. What cap replaces that condition, in which band does the order state the new cap, and what GSO arc exclusion does the same waiver require? Answer from DA-26-36. The December 2022 one-beam condition is the condition being removed.
reference:
DA-26-36, adopted and released 9 January 2026. Grant stamp paragraph 4, and the discussion at paragraphs 17 and 19.

The request to remove the condition requiring operation with only one co-frequency, co-polarization beam in any given location in the 12.2-12.7 GHz and 19.7-20.2 GHz bands is GRANTED. An answer that says the December 2022 one-beam condition still applies in those two bands is wrong.

text: A new crew member is told on launch day that the government has not certified the vehicle. Is that on time, and does someone who was already employed on 23 December 2004 follow the same clock?
reference:
14 CFR 460.9. An operator must inform in writing any individual serving as crew that the United States Government has not certified the launch vehicle and any reentry vehicle as safe for carrying flight crew or space flight participants.

For a person who was not already employed as crew on 23 December 2004, that writing is due before the operator enters into any contract or other arrangement to employ the individual. Launch day is late. The disclosure is a condition of the employment arrangement, not a briefing at the pad.

For a crew member employed as of 23 December 2004, the writing is due as early as possible and prior to any launch in which that individual will participate as crew. That person does not follow the before-hire clock. A crew member hired after that date does not get the 2004 clock.

Wrong: every crew member may be told on launch day. Wrong: a person employed on 23 December 2004 had to be told before being hired.

text: If destroying the vehicle would put more people at risk than letting it fly, do the flight-safety limits still require an abort, and does a lost track force one?
reference:
14 CFR 450.108, which applies when flight abort is used as a hazard control to meet 14 CFR 450.101.

The flight-safety limits must be designed to avoid a flight abort that increases collective risk to the public in uncontrolled areas, compared with continued flight. An abort is not required merely because it is available. If aborting would raise that collective risk, the limits are written to avoid the abort.

A lost track does not by itself force an abort. The flight safety system must abort when tracking data is invalid and further flight has the potential to violate a flight safety limit, using the methods that account for losing the data needed to evaluate the abort rules. It must also abort when valid real-time data show a flight-safety limit has been violated, and when the vehicle state approaches a condition expected to compromise the flight safety system if further flight could violate a limit.

Which flight-safety-system standard applies depends on the consequence. Greater than 1 × 10−2 conditional expected casualties in uncontrolled areas, from any reasonably foreseeable failure mode in any significant period of flight, requires a system meeting 14 CFR 450.145. A consequence between 1 × 10−2 and 1 × 10−3 requires a system meeting 14 CFR 450.143. The section does not assign either standard below that lower figure.

Abort to protect against a high-consequence event in uncontrolled areas does not have to continue for the whole flight. It can end immediately after critical vehicle parameters are validated, if the vehicle can still achieve a useful mission, abort would not materially decrease the risk from that high-consequence event, and there are no key flight-safety events for the rest of the flight.

In place of the useful-mission and 1 × 10−2 objectives in 450.108(c)(2) and (c)(4), the operator may instead keep debris capable of causing a casualty out of uncontrolled areas with a flight safety system that meets 450.145.

Wrong: the vehicle must be destroyed whenever it leaves the planned path. Wrong: invalid tracking always means abort. Wrong: every flight uses the highly reliable abort standard through landing.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-III/subchapter-C/part-450/subpart-C/section-450.108

text: If the Space Bureau determines that Gen2 operations under the January 2026 EPFD waiver have caused harmful interference, may SpaceX keep the higher power while it studies the complaint, and can the Bureau take the waiver back?
reference:
DA-26-36 grant stamp on the EPFD waiver, and paragraph 17.

If the Space Bureau notifies SpaceX of a determination that it has caused harmful interference, SpaceX must immediately return to operating in accordance with the Commission's EPFD limits in the affected frequency bands. SpaceX must also communicate to its affected customers how it is rectifying the situation if that mediation will affect their service.

The grant stamp says the Space Bureau will revoke the waiver in the event of unresolved harmful interference. Paragraph 17 says the Space Bureau may revoke the waiver in that event. Both sentences are in the order. An answer that reports only one of those verbs should say which sentence it is using.

Wrong: SpaceX may keep operating above the EPFD limits while it studies the complaint. Wrong: the waiver cannot be revoked.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt

text: DA-26-36 authorizes Gen2 W-band operations in 92.0-94.0, 94.1-95.0, 95.0-100.0, 102.0-109.5, and 111.8-114.25 GHz. Are those operations a protected downlink, and what minimum earth-station elevation does the order require at each satellite altitude?
reference:
DA-26-36 paragraph 9, footnote 21, and paragraph 11.

The Bureau grants a waiver of the U.S. Table for global uplink (Earth-to-space) communications in 92.0-94.0 GHz, 94.1-95.0 GHz, 95.0-100.0 GHz, 102.0-109.5 GHz, and 111.8-114.25 GHz, on an unprotected and non-interference basis. Footnote 21: operations in those W-band frequencies are non-conforming with the International Table of Frequency Allocations and are on an unprotected, non-interference basis under ITU Radio Regulations Article 4.4.

Paragraph 11: SpaceX seeks to use the W-band frequencies on a receive-only basis, meaning the satellite receives the uplink. The W-band earth stations will have a minimum elevation angle of 10 degrees for satellites operating below 400 km, 20 degrees for satellites operating between 400 km and 500 km, and 25 degrees for satellites operating above 500 km. Operations under the waiver are unprotected and non-interference.

Wrong: these W-band operations have primary status under the International Table. Wrong: the grant is a space-to-Earth downlink. Wrong: the order sets no elevation floor.

Source: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-36A1.txt

text: The FCC adopted new NEPA rules on 30 September 2026 declaring that space-based operations are not major federal actions, and six days later it authorized SpaceX's 15,000-satellite D2D constellation over DarkSky International's environmental objection. Did the Bureaus apply the new NEPA rules to that authorization? Explain which rule framework they used, how they treated DarkSky's letter, when the new rules take effect, what the new rule text (section 1.1302) says about launches, and who the order says is responsible for launch and re-entry effects. News reports describe a 2-1 vote; check what the order's caption says about the dissent.
reference:
Grade two documents: FCC-26-64 (Modernizing the Commission's NEPA Rules, WT Docket 25-217, Report and Order and FNPRM, adopted 30 September 2026, released 1 October 2026) and DA-26-1078 (6 October 2026) paragraph 45 and footnotes 136-146.

Did the Bureaus apply the new rules? No. DA-26-1078 paragraph 45: the new rules "do not come into effect until 30 days after publication in the Federal Register or after conclusion of the Paperwork Reduction Act process", so the Bureaus "review these comments under our current rules", find the action categorically excluded under 47 CFR 1.1306(a), and decline to require further NEPA review. Footnote 140: DarkSky's letter is treated as a petition for environmental review under 47 CFR 1.1307(c). The paragraph notes that under the new framework the authorization would not require NEPA review and the comments would be moot, but that is dicta; the operative basis is the current categorical exclusion. Footnotes 142-143: the FAA conducts environmental review of launches; an agency need not duplicate another agency's review (47 CFR 1.1311(e)). Footnote 145 calls the aluminum-oxide claim speculative.

FCC-26-64: paragraphs 62-65 find Commission-licensed space-based operations are "extraterritorial activities" excluded from the MFA definition (42 U.S.C. 4336e(10)(B)(vi)) and that spectrum authorizations do not create federal control over deployments. New section 1.1302(c)(5): "Actions associated with space-based operations, including the launch, deployment, and operation of space stations" are not Commission MFAs; 1.1302(b)(6) codifies the extraterritorial exclusion. Footnote 201: the FAA is charged by statute (51 U.S.C. 50903) with licensing launches and controlled re-entries, and the FCC does not view NEPA as giving it authority superseding the FAA's. Paragraph 221: the Report and Order, including revised 1.1301 and 1.1302, is effective 30 days after Federal Register publication; other Appendix A revisions wait for OMB PRA approval and a WTB notice. Caption: "Commissioner Gomez dissenting in part and issuing a statement" - a partial dissent, not a full one; SatNews reported "voted 2-1".

Wrong answers: that the D2D grant relied on the new 1.1302 exclusion; that the new rules were effective on 1 or 6 October 2026; that the FCC now reviews launch emissions; that DarkSky's filing was ignored rather than treated as a 1.1307(c) petition; that the vote was unanimous.

Sources: https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-26-64A1.pdf ; https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-1078A1.pdf

text: The FCC's April 2026 NGSO-GSO sharing order replaced EPFD limits with performance criteria and added a minimum GSO-arc avoidance angle. For a SpaceX analyst: what is the rule's minimum avoidance angle and the equivalent exclusion zone, in which bands does it apply, may an NGSO operator start service while its compliance demonstration is still pending, and what are the three numerical protection criteria? Then compare that with the GSO-arc exclusion the 6 October 2026 D2D grant actually imposes on SpaceX until the new rules are effective. Finally, when do the rules take effect and which two sections are carved out? Do not conflate the rule's angle with the angle in SpaceX's waiver condition.
reference:
Grade FCC-26-26 (Modernizing Spectrum Sharing for Satellite Broadband, SB Docket 25-157, adopted 30 April 2026, released 1 May 2026) paragraphs 50, 54, 59-65, footnote 225 and ordering clause 90, plus DA-26-1078 (6 October 2026) grant condition 11.

Rule: paragraph 63 - NGSO systems in the 10.7-12.7, 17.3-18.6 and 19.7-20.2 GHz bands must observe a 3-degree GSO-arc avoidance angle with respect to any operational co-frequency GSO satellite serving the United States. Footnote 225: 3 degrees measured on either side of the GSO satellite equals a total 6-degree GSO-arc avoidance zone. Paragraph 64: applicants may submit technical demonstrations and begin operating on an unprotected, non-interference basis while the demonstrations are pending, provided they operate within the demonstrated parameters and the 3-degree angle. Paragraph 65: the Commission may revisit the requirement.

Criteria: paragraph 50 - long-term 3% time-weighted average degraded throughput for GSO links using ACM; paragraph 54 - short-term 0.1% absolute increase in link unavailability (more protective than the 0.4% used in NGSO-NGSO sharing); paragraphs 59-61 - for non-ACM links, -10.5 dB I/N not to be exceeded for 80% of the time, applied in Ku and Ka bands. 328 GSO reference links (paragraph 67); Space Bureau to open a reference-link proceeding within 15 days of release (paragraph 69).

SpaceX D2D grant: DA-26-1078 condition 11(a) requires a minimum GSO arc exclusion zone of at least FOUR degrees with respect to operational GSO satellites, until the new rules are effective and SpaceX demonstrates compliance; 11(b) operations outside the U.S. must meet the EPFD limits unless another country authorizes otherwise; 11(c) unprotected, non-interference, must return to EPFD limits on a Bureau determination of harmful interference, waiver revocable; 11(d) must share ITU validation input data until a favorable or qualified favorable ITU finding. So the waiver condition (4 degrees) is stricter than the rule's 3-degree minimum; an answer that says SpaceX operates under a 3-degree angle today, or that the rule sets 4 degrees, is wrong.

Effective date: ordering clause 90 - effective 60 days after Federal Register publication, except sections 25.146(a)(3) and 25.289(a)(2), which await OMB Paperwork Reduction Act review and a Space Bureau Federal Register notice. The Federal Register summary appeared 13 May 2026 (2026-09565); DA-26-1078 footnote 131 confirms the rules were not yet effective on 6 October 2026 as to those sections.

text: The FCC adopted its Satellite Spectrum Abundance order on 30 September 2026 (released 1 October 2026, FCC-26-65). Press says it 'unlocks 1,050 MHz' including '550 MHz for downlinks to consumer dishes' in 12.7-13.25 GHz. From the order itself: how many megahertz does the Commission say it unlocks in the 12.7 GHz band, what may NGSO systems do in the band and on what interference footing relative to uplink earth stations, which uplinks remain allowed and from whom, what happens to the application freeze in 12.7-12.75 GHz versus 12.75-13.25 GHz, and when do grandfathered fixed and mobile licensees drop to secondary status. Also give the 42 GHz allocation direction and earth-station licensing type, and the effective-date rule with its exceptions. Note whether Starlink can use the band immediately.
reference:
Grade FCC-26-65 (SB Docket 25-180 et al., adopted 30 September 2026, released 1 October 2026), paragraphs 15-19, 22-26, 29-30, 36-38, footnotes 62, 66, 72, and ordering clauses 132 and 134.

Megahertz: paragraphs 15-16 - "525 megahertz" of additional, contiguous downlink spectrum in the 12.7 GHz band, "a more than 25% increase". The 550 and 1,050 MHz figures in press coverage (TeslaNorth, 30 Sept 2026) are not the order's figures; the order says 525 MHz for 12.7 GHz and 500 MHz for 42 GHz.

NGSO: new primary FSS (space-to-Earth) allocation for NGSO systems in 12.7-13.25 GHz (new footnote NG144), with blanket licensing of user terminals and ESIMs on land, sea and air (paragraphs 15, 18). NGSO FSS downlinks must accept any interference from FSS uplinks from gateway or feeder-link earth stations and operate unprotected vis-a-vis grandfathered terrestrial stations (paragraphs 15, 18). PFD limits from 10.7-11.7 GHz are extended (paragraph 19).

Uplinks: limited to individually licensed gateway and feeder-link earth stations communicating with GSO and NGSO space stations (paragraph 23), plus blanket-licensed ESIMs on aircraft at altitude and ships away from the coast communicating with GSO satellites only (paragraphs 25-26). No ESIM uplinks to NGSO. The "international systems only" limit on GSO uplinks (NG52) is removed (paragraph 22).

Freezes: footnote 62 - the temporary freeze on 12.75-13.25 GHz applications is lifted effective upon Federal Register publication (procedural, no APA delay); paragraph 24 and footnote 72 - 12.7-12.75 GHz gets a permanent freeze on new FSS (Earth-to-space) space and earth station applications via NG144, as a buffer for 12.2-12.7 GHz DBS and FSS downlinks.

Incumbents: paragraphs 29-30 and ordering clause 134 - existing FS and MS licensees are grandfathered co-primary for 10 years from Federal Register publication, after which they become secondary (unprotected, non-harmful-interference basis); the Order of Proposed Modification under section 316 gives licensees 30 days from publication to protest; overall FS/MS allocations change to secondary.

42 GHz: paragraph 36-37 - primary FSS space-to-Earth (downlink only) for GSO and NGSO, to individually licensed and Nationwide Non-Site licensed gateway/feeder-link earth stations (new NG150), no blanket licensing, PFD limits extended from 40.5-42 GHz; MS allocation changed to secondary (paragraph 38); light licensing (paragraph 39).

Effective: ordering clause 132 - 60 days after Federal Register publication, except sections 100.212(c), (i), (j), 100.275(n) and (o), which await OMB review and a Space Bureau notice. Note the rules are written into part 100 even though part 100 is not yet effective (Background section, which states the Commission amends part 100 sections rather than part 25 because part 25 will be removed once part 100 is effective). Starlink cannot use the band immediately: it needs a modification of its space station authorization (SpaceX already requested 12.7-13.25 GHz in DA-26-36, conditions 2-3, and the Gen3 application SAT-LOA-20260630-00264 is pending, per footnotes 140 and 143).

Wrong answers: 550 or 1,050 MHz as the order's figure; NGSO uplinks from user terminals; ESIM uplinks to NGSO; terrestrial incumbents made secondary immediately; 42 GHz allowed for uplinks or blanket-licensed terminals.

Alternatives: the FAA selected the Preferred Alternative (issue a new vehicle operator license or modify an existing license for up to 44 launches and 88 landings per year, 44 per stage, plus about 800,000 sq ft of infrastructure).
